chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Abu al-Subah ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:
By Allah, that which Al-Hasan ibn Ali (peace be upon him) did was better for this community than all that upon which the sun rises.
By Allah, this Verse was revealed:

Have you not seen those to whom it was said: Withhold your hands [from fighting], and establish prayer, and give zakah? But when fighting is prescribed for them, you see of them a few [only] fearing people as they ought to fear Allah, or [even] a greater fear.

It is merely the obedience to the Imam. And they sought battle, but when battle was prescribed for them alongside Al-Husayn (peace be upon him), they said: 'Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? Why did You not delay us to a near term? We would answer Your call and follow the Messengers.'
They intended to delay that to Al-Qa'im (peace be upon him).

key_terms.الْحَسَنُ بْنُ عَلِيٍ: Al-Hasan ibn Ali, the second Imam

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of Al-Hasan ibn Ali's action in relation to the Quranic verse of those who sought to delay fighting?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) asserts that Hasan ibn al-Husayn’s decision to remain in quietude rather than engage in armed conflict was superior for the Ummah, interpreting the reluctance of the companions in Surah al-Nisa’ (4:77) as a desire to await the final Imam, Al-Qa'im. This narration highlights the Shia theological distinction between the political prudence of Hasan’s peace treaty and the martyrdom-focused resistance of Husayn, framing the 'delay' mentioned in the verse as an eschatological expectation of the Mahdi. It underscores the principle that obedience to the Imam’s specific strategic choice—whether war or peace—is the ultimate form of religious compliance.
